name: Riang Lang / Rianglang
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.

catalog_locator: Luce MS 6547 Box 7 Folder 64 p. 053, paragraph headed 'Unaccented Penultimates' (page footer 'Luce Collection, MS 6547, Box 7, Folder 64, Page 053. National Library of Australia'); Shorto 2013 p. ii, 2nd paragraph; Hall 2018 p. 83 sec. 4 'Word structure'
catalog_quote: Luce ms p. 053 (my transcription): "Unaccented Penultimates. The accent in R.L. always falls on the [one word struck out] last syllable. There are plenty of monosyllables, whether original monosyllables or not I cannot say. There are also plenty of dissyllables, the marked feature of which is that they always carry the Low Tone and the neutral vowel -ə. The initial consonant in these unaccented syllables is never aspirated [interlinear insertion: (if we except -sᶜ-, which is always aspirated as in Shan, not in Burma)], & is practically confined to k-, ts-, t-, p-, r- & sᶜ-. ... There are indications that these final consonants, being in unaccented syllables, tend to drop off, leaving merely the neutral vowel." Same page, note beside the consonant table: "Aspirated plosives pᶜ, tᶜ, kᶜ [struck word, 'not so' written above] common as the unaspirated, & confined to accented initials (the main syllable), but much commoner than in Mon." Shorto 2013 p. ii: "The pitch of prefixial syllables is always low, and this is not specially marked. Low pitch is probably generally connected with absence of stress; it is frequent in particles and the first syllables of compounds, and is marked in such cases." Hall 2018 p. 83: "Riang Lang is sesquisyllabic; words include a main syllable and an optional reduced syllable preceding the main syllable. ... The reduced syllable has a limited inventory of consonants, and vowel and tone are neutralized."
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Riang Lang is a two-tone language with sesquisyllabic words: a full main syllable optionally preceded by one reduced (prefixal/minor) syllable with a neutral vowel and no tone contrast. Word accent/stress falls on the main syllable, which is always the last syllable of the word; the preceding minor syllable is unaccented (low pitch, neutral vowel, reduced consonant inventory, final consonants tending to drop). Effectively fixed final (= main-syllable) stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None for word accent. Luce (ms p. 050) notes some common words seem to have no fixed tone; Shorto (p. ii) notes low pitch also in particles and first syllables of compounds and 'disturbance of lexical tone' in doubled roots.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, based on elicited wordlists (Luce's field notes, 1930s-50s; Hall's 1537-item list from Sam Kha village, Namsang township, 2015-17). Luce's statement is an unpublished manuscript note; Hall 2018, the only Glottolog-listed description, never uses the word stress and describes only tone and sesquisyllabic structure.
new_statements.identity_note: All three statements concern Riang Lang = Yinnet / Black Riang (ISO ril, rian1261): Luce's 'R.L.' is Riang-Lang (his Riang Sak/Riang Lai material is the sister variety Yinchia, ISO yin, glottocode yinc1238). Hall 2018 describes the Riang Lang of Sam Kha village, Namsang township, southern Shan State; Luce's notes come from his own 1930s-50s fieldwork (informant U San Mya for the Riang Sak-Riang Lang lexicon); Shintani 2014 (not seen) covers a Riang Lang variety near Löy Lëm, Panglong. Riang Lang and Riang Lai are reported mutually intelligible.

tone_statements.citation: Shorto, H. L. 1963. The structural patterns of northern Mon-Khmer languages. In H. L. Shorto (ed.), Linguistic Comparison in South East Asia and the Pacific, 45-61. London: SOAS.
tone_statements.quote: The word consists, in Palaung, of a major syllable which may be prece by one or two minor ones ; in Riang-Lang, of a major syllable which is acc panied by either term of a two-tone system, and may be preceded by one or minor syllables … putting Ma a major syllable, Mi for a minor one, T for tone … These point to an old NMK voiced /voiceless distinction in initial plosives which has survived as such only in Palaung, being replaced by a distinction of low and high tone in Riang-Lang and lost in Praok except in the context of certain vowels, where it has been replaced by one of vowel quality.
tone_statements.locator: p. 46 'Word patterns' and p. 49 'Comparison: (1) Plosive distinctions'; cf. p. 53 Morphology
tone_statements.summary: Two tones, low and high, one per word carried with the major syllable (minor syllables toneless); the contrast continues an old initial voicing distinction; prefixation can change the tone.

tone_statements.quote: Rianglang Tones (i) High level, often high-circumflex in the sentence, (ii) Falling, often looping at the end of a clause ... After a low tone, the sudden change to a high one seems difficult for a Riang speaker, so I often omit a tonal m[ark] in such cases, where the high level does not seem to be attained. And there are certain common words ... which seem to me to have no fixed tone. ... To explain, therefore, the two tones of Rianglan[g] as a Mon-Khmer language (usually assumed to be Non-Tonal), one begins by seeing if the low tone c[an be] the hallmark of an original sonant initial. - After comparing 58 words common to Palaung & Riang ... I find that this rule works in 38 instances

tone.quote: … the observations of G. H. Luce on Riang and of K. G. Izikowitz on Lamet should rather be interpreted in another way. … It is not unlikely that Riang and Lamet are actually voice register languages rather than tone languages. … Comparing Danaw with Riang, Luce observed that the low tone of Riang corresponds to the high falling tone of Danaw, but that the high tone of Riang corresponds to two distinct Danaw tones: low falling and high level, the latter for words which in Riang retain a final glottal closure that has disappeared in Danaw.
